qs.q: Administration of salicylates to a child with a specific viral infection can lead to fulminant encephalitis associated with Reye's syndrome. Which virus is implicated?
qs.e: Fulminant encephalitis can occur as a rare complication of varicella and may be part of Reye's syndrome if salicylates are administered. Other herpesviruses like CMV or EBV are not classically linked to salicylate-induced Reye's syndrome.

faq.a: Aspirin uncouples mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, worsening the metabolic stress of viral infection and leading to fatty liver and cerebral edema.

exam: A 6‑year‑old with varicella was given aspirin and now has vomiting and lethargy – what is your immediate management? — Stop aspirin, secure airway, give IV dextrose, start measures to reduce intracranial pressure.
How does the liver histology in Reye syndrome differ from that in viral hepatitis? — Microvesicular fatty change without necrosis versus hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation.

What laboratory pattern distinguishes Reye syndrome from sepsis‑related liver failure? — Mild‑moderate transaminase rise with high ammonia and normal white cell count; sepsis often shows marked leukocytosis and bilirubin rise.
Why is hypoglycaemia a critical early sign, and how should it be corrected? — Impaired β‑oxidation limits gluconeogenesis; give rapid IV dextrose bolus followed by continuous infusion.

A child presents with encephalopathy after influenza; aspirin use is unknown. Which question in the history is most discriminating? — Ask specifically about any antipyretic or analgesic given, especially aspirin.
What are the contraindicated drugs in a child with suspected Reye syndrome and why? — Aspirin (causes), other salicylates (same mechanism); avoid hepatotoxic drugs like high‑dose paracetamol.
Explain why a normal ALT does not rule out Reye syndrome. — The hepatic injury is functional (mitochondrial) rather than necrotic, so transaminases may be only modestly elevated.
In a low‑resource setting without ammonia testing, what clinical sign suggests hepatic encephalopathy? — Flapping tremor (asterixis) and worsening asterixis with mental status decline.
ai.title: Reye Syndrome
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Acute, fatal encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction in children after viral illness treated with aspirin. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by labs showing microvesicular steatosis and elevated ammonia.

b: Occurs in children <15 years, peak 4‑12 y
Pathogenesis: mitochondrial dysfunction → impaired β‑oxidation → microvesicular fatty change
sections.p: Reye syndrome is a rare, rapidly progressive metabolic encephalopathy that follows a viral infection (most often influenza or varicella) when a child receives aspirin. It is characterised by cerebral edema and hepatic failure without necrosis.

b: Rapidly worsening headache, vomiting, lethargy → coma
sections.p: The syndrome manifests as a fulminant encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction. Multi‑organ involvement (myositis, cardiac dysfunction) may appear later.

b: History of recent viral illness and aspirin exposure
Exclusion of meningitis, viral encephalitis, metabolic disorders, sepsis
sections.p: No single test confirms Reye syndrome; diagnosis is clinical, after excluding other causes of encephalopathy and liver failure.

t.b: Is hepatic encephalopathy present? High ammonia (>100 µmol/L) supports diagnosis

t.a: Liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin, INR)
t.b: Do we have hepatic dysfunction? Mild‑moderate rise in AST/ALT, INR > 1.5
Is hypoglycaemia contributing? Glucose < 3 mmol/L needs correction
Rule out infectious meningitis; normal CSF favours Reye
Look for fatty liver; microvesicular steatosis is typical but not always visible

b: Control intracranial pressure: head elevation, mannitol or hypertonic saline
Correct coagulopathy with fresh frozen plasma if bleeding risk
sections.p: Management is supportive intensive care; no specific antidote exists. Early removal of aspirin and aggressive control of cerebral edema are priorities.

b: Always ask about aspirin or salicylate use in a child with flu/varicella
Encephalopathy with mild transaminase rise → think Reye, not hepatitis
sections.p: Key points examiners love: link aspirin use to viral prodrome, recognise microvesicular fatty change, differentiate from viral encephalitis and septic shock, and outline ICU‑level supportive measures.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of raised intracranial pressure (bulging fontanelle, papilledema)
